messages.subject: Re: Final Length of Animal
messages.body_plain:
That makes more sense! Thank you for the help!

On Friday, October 29, 2021 at 6:30:08 PM UTC-4 NicheMapR wrote:
> Hi Tripp,
>
> You found a bug! It was the final wet mass that was going into the last column of yearout, not the final length. I've fixed it now and pushed the changes to github. Below is an example of the desert tortoise simulated at the Desert Center in CA, using micro_global (you'd have to change your folder for the allstat.Rda file). Note that below I've removed the shade definition as it comes straight from the microclimate model and I've put kap.X in place of kap_X and put the code defining potentially missing Arrhenius parameters based on CT_min and CT_max after the specification of the latter.
>
> nyear <- 50
> micro <- micro_global(nyears = nyear, loc = c(-115.4, 33.7), timeinterval = 365)
>
> load('c:/git/AmPtool/allStat.Rda')
>
> species <- "Gopherus.agassizii"
> allDEB.species <- unlist(labels(allStat$allStat))
> allDEB.species <- allDEB.species [1 : (length(allDEB.species) - 2)]
> species.slot <- which(allDEB.species == species)
> par.names <- unlist(labels(allStat$allStat[[species.slot]]))
> # clear possible missing parameters
> if(exists("E.Hj")==TRUE){rm(E.Hj)}
> if(exists("E.He")==TRUE){rm(E.He)}
> if(exists("L.j")==TRUE){rm(L.j)}
> if(exists("T.L")==TRUE){rm(T.L)}
> if(exists("T.H")==TRUE){rm(T.H)}
> if(exists("T.AL <http://T.AL>")==TRUE){rm(T.AL <http://T.AL>)}
> if(exists("T.AH")==TRUE){rm(T.AH)}
>
> for(i in 1:length(par.names)){
>   assign(par.names[i], unlist(allStat$allStat[[species.slot]][i]))
> }
>
> # assign possible missing parameters
> if(exists("E.Hj")==FALSE){E.Hj <- E.Hb}
> if(exists("E.He")==FALSE){E.He <- E.Hb}
> if(exists("L.j")==FALSE){L.j <- L.b}
> p_Xm <- p.Am / kap.X # redefining p_Xm to max possible value
>
> z.mult <- 1 # DEB body size scaling parameter
>
> # overwrite nitrogenous waste indices with those of uric acid (currently ammonia by default)
> n.NC <- 1
> n.NH <- 4/5
> n.NO <- 3/5
> n.NN <- 4/5
>
> # morph, behav and water loss
> Ww_g <- 4500 # wet weight of animal (g) *estimate
> pct_wet <- 0.05 # % of surface area acting as a free-water exchanger
> alpha_max <- 0.82 # maximum solar absorptivity
> alpha_min <- 0.82 # minimum solar absorptivity
> shape <- 0 # animal shape - 0 = Plate
> T_RB_min <- 15 # min Tb at which they will attempt to leave retreat
> T_B_min <- 15 # min Tb at which leaves retreat to bask
> T_F_min <- 19 # minimum Tb at which activity occurs
> T_F_max <- 38 # maximum Tb at which activity occurs
> T_pref <- 30 # preferred Tb (will try and regulate to this)
> CT_max <- 43 # critical thermal minimum (affects choice of retreat)
> CT_min <- 8 # critical thermal maximum (affects choice of retreat)
> mindepth <- 2 # min depth (node, 1-10) allowed
> maxdepth <- 10 # max depth (node, 1-10) allowed
> shade_seek <- 1 # shade seeking?
> burrow <- 1 # can it burrow?
> climb <- 0 # can it climb to thermoregulate?
> minshade <- 0 # min available shade?
> nocturn <- 0 # nocturnal activity
> crepus <- 0 # crepuscular activity
> diurn <- 1 # diurnal activity
>
> # assign missing 5-par thermal response curve parameters if necessary
> if(exists("T.L")==FALSE){T.L <- 0 + 273.15}
> if(exists("T.H")==FALSE){T.H <- 50 + 273.15}
>
> if(exists("T.AL <http://T.AL>")==FALSE){T.AL <http://T.AL> <- 5E04}
> if(exists("T.AH")==FALSE){T.AH <- 9E04}
>
> # DEB initial state
> # egg
> #V_init <- 3e-9
> #E_init <- E.0 / V_init
> #E_H_init <- 0
> #stage <- 0
>
> # hatchling
> # V_init <- L.b^3
> # E_init <- E.m
> # E_H_init <- E.Hb
> # stage <- 1
>
>
> # mature
> V_init <- L.p^3
> E_init <- E.m
> E_H_init <- E.Hp+2
> stage <- 2
>
> viviparous <- 0 # live bearing (1) or egg laying (0)
> clutchsize <- 5 # how many eggs per clutch?
> photostart <- 3 # winter solstice is the start of the reproduction cycle
> photofinish <- 2 # autumnal equinox is the end of the reproduction cycle
>
> # run the ectotherm model
> ecto<-ectotherm(DEB=1,
>                 viviparous=viviparous,
>                 clutchsize=clutchsize,
>                 z.mult=z.mult,
>                 shape=shape,
>                 alpha_max=alpha_max,
>                 alpha_min=alpha_min,
>                 T_F_min=T_F_min,
>                 T_F_max=T_F_max,
>                 T_B_min=T_B_min,
>                 T_RB_min=T_RB_min,
>                 T_pref=T_pref,
>                 CT_max=CT_max,
>                 CT_min=CT_min,
>                 diurn=diurn,
>                 nocturn=nocturn,
>                 crepus=crepus,
>                 shade_seek=shade_seek,
>                 burrow=burrow,
>                 climb=climb,
>                 mindepth=mindepth,
>                 maxdepth=maxdepth,
>                 pct_wet=pct_wet,
>                 z=z*z.mult,
>                 del_M=del.M,
>                 p_Xm = p.Xm,
>                 kap_X=kap.X,
>                 v=v/24,
>                 kap=kap,
>                 p_M=p.M/24,
>                 E_G=E.G,
>                 kap_R=kap.R,
>                 k_J=k.J/24,
>                 E_Hb=E.Hb*z.mult^3,
>                 E_Hj=E.Hj*z.mult^3,
>                 E_Hp=E.Hp*z.mult^3,
>                 E_He=E.He*z.mult^3,
>                 h_a=h.a/(24^2),
>                 s_G=s.G,
>                 T_REF=T.ref,
>                 T_A=T.A,
>                 T_AL=T.AL <http://T.AL>,
>                 T_AH=T.AH,
>                 T_L=T.L,
>                 T_H=T.H,
>                 E_0=E.0*z.mult^4,
>                 f=f,
>                 d_V=d.V,
>                 d_E=d.E,
>                 d_Egg=d.E,
>                 mu_X=mu.X,
>                 mu_E=mu.E,
>                 mu_V=mu.V,
>                 mu_P=mu.P,
>                 kap_X_P=kap.P,
>                 n_X=c(n.CX,n.HX,n.OX,n.ON),
>                 n_E=c(n.CE,n.HE,n.OE,n.OE),
>                 n_V=c(n.CV,n.HV,n.OV,n.OV),
>                 n_P=c(n.CP,n.HP,n.OP,n.OP),
>                 n_M_nitro=c(n.NC,n.NH,n.NO,n.NN),
>                 L_b=L.b,
>                 V_init=V_init,
>                 E_init=E_init,
>                 E_H_init=E_H_init,
>                 stage=stage,
>                 photostart = photostart,
>                 photofinish = photofinish)
>
> # retrieve output
> environ<-as.data.frame(ecto$environ)     # behaviour, Tb and environment
> enbal<-as.data.frame(ecto$enbal)         # heat balance outputs
> masbal<-as.data.frame(ecto$masbal)       # mass balance outputs
> debout<-as.data.frame(ecto$debout)       # DEB model outputs
> yearout <- as.data.frame(ecto$yearout)   # whole life cycle summary
> yearsout <- as.data.frame(ecto$yearsout) # annual summaries
>
> yearout
> plot(micro$dates / 365, debout$L_W, type = 'l', ylab = 'plastron length, mm', xlab = 'years')
>
>
>
>
>

> > > > > Hi - the DEB parameter that converts structural lengths to physical lengths is 'del.M'. The z.mult parameter allows you to scale the organism up and down in size according to the DEB covariation rules (whereby size at birth, size at puberty, maximum size, egg size and longevity all scale together in a particular way).
> > > > >
> > > > > But I don't think you need to change anything if you're aiming to simulate the Desert Tortoise. The length is in mm and represents plastron length in this case. If you play around with this app http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/deb/ choosing the Desert Tortoise, you'll see it gives sensible lengths, as does the ectotherm function. Perhaps it was simply that you didn't realize it was mm? Or did you want to simulate a different species starting from the Desert Tortoise by altering parameters?

Is Pant_Mult in the endoR model the same thing as evaporative cooling capacity? (evaporative cooling capacity as reported here: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/220/18/3290/18700/Avian-thermoregulation-in-the-heat-resting)

Best
Adam
messages.body_snippet:
Hey Mike,

Is Pant_Mult in the endoR model the same thing as evaporative cooling capacity? (evaporative cooling capacity as reported here: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/220/18/3290/18700

messages.subject: Re: Pant_Mult
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

It is an evaporative cooling response - the model is calculating the required breathing rate for the computed metabolic rate (based on the oxygen extraction efficiency and the atmospheric gas concentrations), but you can increase it above this level to invoke evaporative cooling. It can go up to PANT_MAX, so the latter is an indication of evaporative cooling capacity.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Computing solar radiation by SOLRAD
messages.body_plain:
Hi Esther,

If you don't have solar radiation or cloud cover data, you're a bit stuck. SOLRAD is a subroutine in the microclimate model. It computes the clear sky solar from your location and some corrections for aerosols and then the cloud cover input is used to adjust this clear sky estimate. Cloud cover also affects the longwave radiation balance. If you do have solar radiation data, you can estimate cloud cover by seeing how much the observed radiation differs from the clear sky estimate from the microclimate model (i.e. with solonly set to 1 which means it's giving you the output of the subroutine SOLRAD without cloud correction).

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Computing solar radiation by SOLRAD
messages.body_plain:
Hi Esther

You can try using meteorological reanalysis data for the variables that you are missing.  The European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting has produced the ERA-5 reanalysis at a 0.25 degree lat lon grid and 1 hour resolution worldwide.  You can get data from https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/search?type=dataset&text=era5 .  You have to register with them to do downloads but the data are free.  An alternative source is the NCAR/UCAR Research Data Archive in the USA : https://rda.ucar.edu/datasets/ds633.0/.   ERA-5 data are available hourly from 1950 onward.  You can get regional subsets of the data from rda.ucar.edu <http://rda.ucar.edu> or the Copernicus Data Store.

An alternative dataset is NASA  Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2).  See https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/reanalysis/MERRA-2/docs/  for more information. It is hourly from the 1980s, on a  0.625 x 0.5 degree grid.  Regional subsetting is available.

The Japan Meteorological Agency JRA-55 is another possibility.  It is 1958-present, every 3 hours, on a 1.25 degree grid and regional subsets are available. https://rda.ucar.edu/datasets/ds628.0/

All of these datasets have downwelling and upwelling shortwave and longwave radiation in addition to wind speeds, humidity, clouds, temperatures in air, soil and water.  ERA-5 being the highest spatial and temporal resolution is likely to be the most useful.

There are also real-time and near real-time satellite observations of surface temperature, and estimates of downwelling radiation, cloud cover,  and other variables from geostationary satellites.  In Europe, Africa, and the Indian Ocean the EUMETSAT Land Surface Satellite Application Facility produces these sorts of data at 15-min to 1 hour intervals from their two geostationary satellites.  https://landsaf.ipma.pt/en/ .  The EUMETSAT geostationary satellite instrument (SEVIRI) has a 3 km spatial resolution.  NOAA has similar products from their two geostationary satellites over the Americas https://www.goes-r.gov/products/baseline-DSR.html .  The JAXA in Japan operates the Himawari-8 geostationary satellite which is very similar to the two NOAA geostationary satellites and produces similar products over the western Pacific, China and Australasia   https://www.eorc.jaxa.jp/ptree/userguide.html .  In all of these cases you need to register with the websites, but you don't have to pay for the data.  There is pretty much worldwide coverage from these geostationary satellites so you should be able to get data wherever you are working.

Cheers,

David

> All of these datasets have downwelling and upwelling shortwave and longwave radiation in addition to wind speeds, humidity, clouds, temperatures in air, soil and water.  ERA-5 being the highest spatial and temporal resolution is likely to be the most useful.
>
> There are also real-time and near real-time satellite observations of surface temperature, and estimates of downwelling radiation, cloud cover,  and other variables from geostationary satellites.  In Europe, Africa, and the Indian Ocean the EUMETSAT Land Surface Satellite Application Facility produces these sorts of data at 15-min to 1 hour intervals from their two geostationary satellites.  https://landsaf.ipma.pt/en/ .  The EUMETSAT geostationary satellite instrument (SEVIRI) has a 3 km spatial resolution.  NOAA has similar products from their two geostationary satellites over the Americas https://www.goes-r.gov/products/baseline-DSR.html .  The JAXA in Japan operates the Himawari-8 geostationary satellite which is very similar to the two NOAA geostationary satellites and produces similar products over the western Pacific, China and Australasia   https://www.eorc.jaxa.jp/ptree/userguide.html .  In all of these cases you need to register with the websites, but you don't have to pay for the data.  There is pretty much worldwide coverage from these geostationary satellites so you should be able to get data wherever you are working.
>
